planting.note: Direct sow in blocks after soil has warmed, since this variety's main value is its extremely short season rather than yield, so there is little benefit to pushing the planting date earlier than usual.

directions: This is one of the fastest-maturing corns grown in North America, tasseling in about a month and finishing its small 3-4 inch ears well before most other corn has silked, which makes it useful for short, cool growing seasons or for breeding projects needing an early parent. Plant it in blocks of at least four short rows for reliable wind pollination rather than a single long row. Because the plants are compact and finish so quickly, a gardener can often fit in a second planting of another crop afterward, or stagger plantings to extend a short corn harvest window. Dry the small ears fully before shelling; the flint kernels store well and are traditionally soaked and simmered into stews or ground for meal.
sources: Slow Food USA Ark of Taste

common_name: Rhode Island Whitecap Flint Corn (Jonnycake Corn)

planting.note: Direct sow in blocks after soil has warmed; allow the full season to maturity since this is a long-season flint grown for dry cornmeal rather than fresh eating.

directions: This is the flint corn traditionally used to make Rhode Island jonnycakes, a cornmeal flatbread with a legal pedigree: Rhode Island law has at times specified that cornmeal sold for jonnycakes must be ground from whitecap flint grown in the state. Grow it in blocks for wind pollination and expect a single ear per stalk on tall, sturdy plants. Leave ears on the stalk until the husks dry and kernels are rock-hard, then finish curing indoors before shelling and grinding; the kernels have a hard, glassy texture that mills into the coarse, slightly sweet meal classic jonnycake recipes call for.
sources: Slow Food USA Ark of Taste

common_name: Bear Island Flint Corn (Ojibwe Heirloom Flint Corn)

planting.note: Direct sow in blocks once soil has warmed; this variety was adapted for a short northern growing season, so it suits regions with cool summers despite its tall stature.

directions: Bear Island Flint originates with the Ojibwe (Chippewa) of the upper Midwest, traditionally grown on islands in lakes such as Leech Lake where the surrounding water moderated temperatures and reduced losses to animals. Despite its tall, vigorous stalks, it was selected over generations for a growing season short enough for the northern Great Lakes region. Ears carry a striking mix of yellow, red, white, pink, and blue kernels on the same cob. Grow in blocks for pollination and let ears dry fully in the husk before shelling; the multicolor kernels are traditionally processed into hominy or ground into cornmeal.

planting.note: Direct sow in blocks after danger of frost has passed, and isolate from other corn types by distance or timing to keep ears true to the popcorn type.

directions: Calico popcorn produces 5-8 inch ears patterned in red, yellow, brown, purple, and white kernels, making it as popular for fall decorating as for popping. Grow it in blocks of at least four rows for reliable wind pollination, and keep it isolated from sweet corn or field corn plantings since cross-pollination can affect kernel quality on both. Let ears dry fully on the stalk, then finish curing indoors for several weeks until kernels rattle loosely in the husk before shelling and storing. The same decorative ears used for autumn displays can be popped afterward, giving this variety a genuine dual purpose.
